title: Thick and runny liquids, and the skin on water

summary.text: Tip a spoon of water and a spoon of honey together, and the water is gone while the honey crawls. How easily a liquid flows is called its viscosity. Honey has a high viscosity because its particles hold on to each other and slide past each other slowly. Warm honey runs much faster than cool honey, because warmth makes its particles move faster. Water is runny, but its particles attract each other too, and at the top this makes a stretchy skin called surface tension. Water striders, insects with long, hairy, waterproof legs, live on that skin and hunt insects that fall onto ponds.
summary.art: A split picture. On the left, a spoon pouring a thin fast stream of water beside a spoon pouring a slow golden rope of honey that coils on a plate. On the right, a water strider standing on a pond, with small dimples in the water under each foot.

intro.hook: Hold a spoon of water and a spoon of honey over a plate, and tip both at the same moment. The water is gone in a blink. The honey stretches into a slow, shiny rope. Both are liquids. So why does one pour so much more slowly than the other?
intro.text: In this unit you race kitchen liquids down a slope and time each one. You find out what makes a liquid thick or runny, and what warming does to it. Then you look closely at the top of water. There, water acts like a thin stretchy skin. It is strong enough to hold a dome of water on a coin, and to hold up a living insect.
intro.art: A child's two hands tipping a steel spoon of water and a steel spoon of honey over a steel plate. The water splashes flat, the honey hangs in a long golden thread.

outcomes: I can say what viscosity means, and put kitchen liquids in order from runny to thick.
I can run a fair race of liquids down a slope, time each one, and show the results in a table.
I can explain that warming makes most liquids runnier, because their particles move faster and slip past each other more easily.
I can explain surface tension: water particles attract each other, so the top of the water acts like a stretchy skin, and soap makes that skin weaker.
I can explain how a water strider lives on the water's skin: the problem they face, and how their legs and senses help.
I can tell the story of the pitch drop experiment, and explain why something that shatters like a solid can still flow.

terms.meaning: A liquid flows and takes the shape of whatever holds it, but keeps the same amount.
terms.example: Water poured from a jug into a tumbler takes the tumbler's shape.
terms.art: Water poured from a round steel jug into a tall tumbler, taking the tumbler's shape.

terms.meaning: To flow is to move along in a stream, the way a liquid does when it is poured or runs downhill.
terms.example: Rain water flows down the slope of a road into the drain.
terms.art: Rain water running down a sloping street into a drain.

terms.meaning: Viscosity is how much a liquid resists flowing. A liquid with high viscosity flows slowly. A liquid with low viscosity flows fast.
terms.example: Honey has a high viscosity. Water has a low viscosity.
terms.art: Two jars tipped on their sides, one spilling water quickly, the other letting honey ooze out slowly.

terms.meaning: Viscous means thick and slow to flow. It is the scientist's word for a thick liquid.
terms.example: Dosa batter is more viscous than buttermilk.
terms.art: A ladle of thick dosa batter slowly spreading on a tawa.

terms.meaning: Runny means thin and quick to flow, with low viscosity.
terms.example: Rasam is runny. Sambar with lots of dal is thicker.
terms.art: A ladle pouring thin rasam beside a ladle of thick sambar.

terms.meaning: A particle is a tiny piece of a substance, far too small to see. Every solid, liquid and gas is made of particles.
terms.example: A drop of water has more water particles than there are grains of sand on many beaches.
terms.art: A drop of water with a magnified circle showing many small balls jostling together.

terms.meaning: To attract is to pull something closer. Particles of a liquid attract each other.
terms.example: Water particles attract each other, so a drop holds together in a round shape.
terms.art: Small balls with tiny arrows pointing towards each other, holding together in a drop.

terms.meaning: The surface is the outside or top layer of something. The surface of water is where the water meets the air.
terms.example: A dry leaf floats on the surface of a bucket of water.
terms.art: A dry leaf floating on top of the water in a bucket.

terms.meaning: Surface tension is the pull between particles at the surface of a liquid. It makes the surface act like a thin stretchy skin.
terms.example: A one-rupee coin can hold a dome of water drops higher than its edge, because of surface tension.
terms.art: A coin with a tall clear dome of water on top, bulging above the rim of the coin.

terms.meaning: A water strider, also called a pond skater, is an insect with very long legs who lives on the surface of ponds and slow streams.
terms.example: Water striders skate across temple tanks and paddy fields in India.
terms.art: A slim brown insect with six legs, the middle and back legs very long, standing on a pond.

terms.meaning: Pitch is a black, tar-like material made from coal tar or crude oil. It feels hard, but it flows very slowly.
terms.example: Pitch was once used to make boats waterproof.
terms.art: A lump of shiny black pitch in a glass funnel, with one fat drop hanging under it.

terms.meaning: A fair test changes only one thing and keeps everything else the same, so you know what caused the result.
terms.example: In the syrup race, every liquid uses the same spoon, the same slope and the same finish line.
terms.art: Five lanes on a tilted tray, each with the same small blob at the start line.

explanations.concept: Viscosity: how easily a liquid flows
explanations.definition: Viscosity is how much a liquid resists flowing. Thick liquids, like honey, have a high viscosity. Runny liquids, like water, have a low viscosity.
explanations.description: All liquids flow, but not at the same speed. Pour water, oil, shampoo and honey down the same slope, and they arrive in that order. Scientists measure viscosity by timing how long a liquid takes to flow through a narrow tube, or how fast a ball sinks through it. Honey at room warmth has a viscosity thousands of times higher than water. Viscosity is about flowing, not about weight. Coconut oil is more viscous than water, yet it is lighter, so it floats on top of water.
examples: Water runs off a plate at once. Honey takes minutes to slide down the same plate.
Coconut oil pours more slowly than water, but floats on water.
Dosa batter is viscous enough to stay in a round shape on the tawa for a moment.
explanations.art: Four small blobs racing down a tilted steel tray: water already at the bottom, oil near the bottom, shampoo halfway, honey just leaving the start line.
explanations.context: This card says what viscosity means. It is the word scientists use for how thick or runny a liquid is.

explanations.concept: Why honey is thick and water is runny
explanations.definition: The particles in a liquid hold on to each other, but they can slide past each other. When they hold on strongly, or are long and tangled, the liquid flows slowly.
explanations.description: In a liquid, the particles touch, but they are not locked in place as in a solid. They keep sliding past each other, and that is why a liquid flows. Water particles are small and slide past each other easily. Honey is about four parts sugar to one part water. Its sugar particles are much bigger than water particles, and they cling tightly to the water particles and to each other. So they slide past each other slowly. Oil particles are long and much bigger than water particles. Shampoo has long, chain-like particles that tangle like cooked noodles.
examples: Add sugar to water bit by bit, and the water gets thicker: that is how sugar syrup is made.
Kanji, the water rice is cooked in, is thick because of long starch particles from the rice.
Shampoo is made thick on purpose, so it stays in your hand.
explanations.art: Two magnified circles. Left: small water particles sliding past each other freely. Right: honey, with big sugar particles held close to water particles, moving slowly.
explanations.context: This card explains what makes one liquid thick and another runny, at the level of tiny particles.

explanations.definition: When most liquids are warmed, their viscosity goes down, so they flow faster. Warmth makes the particles move faster, so they slip past each other more easily.
explanations.description: The particles in a liquid are always jiggling. Warm the liquid, and they jiggle harder. Then they break away from their neighbours more often, and slide past them more easily. Honey shows this very clearly. Warm a spoon of honey in a bowl of warm water for five minutes, and it runs down a plate many times faster. Cooking oil gets runnier in a hot kadai. A halwai warms thick jaggery syrup so it can be poured. If some liquids get cold enough, they stop flowing and turn solid. Coconut oil turns white and hard in a cool room, below about 24 degrees Celsius.
examples: Warm honey runs fast. Honey from a cold room crawls.
Ghee is soft and thick on a cool morning, and pours easily when warmed.
Coconut oil in a bottle goes white and hard in a cold winter, and melts again in warm water.
explanations.art: Two spoons of honey on a tilted plate: one beside a bowl of warm water, running fast in a long streak, and one at room warmth, a short slow blob.
explanations.context: This card explains why the same liquid flows faster when it is warm. The syrup race tests this with honey.

explanations.concept: Liquids that change when you stir or shake them
explanations.definition: Some liquids get runnier when they are stirred, shaken or squeezed. A few do the opposite and get thicker.
explanations.description: Ketchup is the best known example. Turn a full bottle upside down, and the ketchup often stays put. Shake it or tap the bottle hard, and it suddenly runs. Shaking pulls apart the tiny bits that were holding it in shape. Set curd does something similar. Stir it with a spoon, and it becomes runnier. Paint is made this way on purpose, so it spreads under a brush but does not drip off the wall. A thick paste of cornflour and water does the opposite. It flows when you move it slowly, but turns hard when you punch it. The unit Sorting materials has a test with it.
examples: Ketchup stays in the bottle, then runs when you tap the bottle.
Set curd turns runnier when you stir it well.
Wall paint spreads easily under the brush, then stays where it is put.
explanations.art: A hand tapping the side of an upside-down ketchup bottle, with a sudden blob of ketchup falling onto a plate of samosas.
explanations.context: This card is about liquids whose thickness changes when you stir or shake them, like ketchup and curd.

explanations.concept: The slowest liquids: pitch and ice
explanations.definition: Some materials feel solid but still flow, so slowly that it takes years to notice. Pitch is the most famous example.
explanations.description: Pitch is a black material made from tar. Hit it with a hammer at room temperature and it shatters like glass. Yet it flows. At the University of Queensland in Australia, pitch has been dripping out of a glass funnel since 1930. Only nine drops have fallen so far. The university says pitch is about 100 billion times more viscous than water. Ice also flows when there is a lot of it. A glacier is a huge river of ice, such as the Gangotri glacier in the Himalayas. Its own weight makes it creep slowly downhill. Even the hot rock deep inside the Earth moves very slowly, a few centimetres a year.
examples: In the pitch drop experiment, a drop has fallen about every seven to fourteen years.
A glacier creeps downhill, carrying rocks along with it.
A thick wax candle left in a hot car can sag and bend over hours.
explanations.art: A glass funnel full of black pitch under a glass dome, one fat black drop hanging below it, and a calendar on the wall with many years crossed out.
explanations.context: This card is about materials that look solid but flow, very slowly. It tells about pitch and glaciers.

explanations.concept: Surface tension: the skin on water
explanations.definition: Surface tension is the pull between particles at the surface of a liquid. It makes the surface act like a thin stretchy skin.
explanations.description: Water particles attract each other. Deep inside the water, each particle is pulled equally from every side. At the surface there is only air above, and air pulls very little. So the surface particles are pulled down and sideways, towards their neighbours. They hold together like a stretched sheet. That is why a drop is round, and why a coin can hold a dome of water above its edge. Soap makes the skin much weaker. Oil has a weaker skin than water, so oil drops spread out flatter. The units Biomimicry and How water climbs a plant say more about water's pull.
examples: Drops of water pile up on a coin into a dome before they spill over.
A drop of soap breaks the skin, and the dome spills at once.
A loop of thread on water snaps into a circle when soap touches inside it.
explanations.art: A side view of water in a glass with a magnified circle at the top: surface particles pulled down and sideways by their neighbours, forming a skin.
explanations.context: This card explains surface tension, the pull at the top of water that makes it act like a skin.

explanations.concept: Water striders: insects who live on the water's skin
explanations.definition: A water strider is an insect who lives on the surface of still or slow water. Their legs are long, and covered in tiny waxy hairs that keep water off, so the water's skin holds them up.
explanations.description: Many small insects fall onto ponds by accident: ants, flies, small moths. They struggle and cannot get off. That is food for anyone who can reach them, but reaching them means standing on water without sinking. A water strider does this. Their legs are covered in thousands of tiny hairs with a waxy coat, and air is trapped between the hairs. Water cannot wet the legs, so each foot only presses a small dent in the water's skin. Their long legs spread their weight over a wide area. Water striders feel ripples through their legs. A struggling insect sends out ripples, and the strider turns and skates to it, then grabs the prey with their short front legs. Many water striders also send ripple signals to each other by tapping the water.
examples: Water striders rush to an ant that has fallen into a temple tank.
Under a water strider, you can see small round dents in the water, and their shadows on the bottom.
Sea skaters, a kind of water strider, live on the open ocean, far from land.
explanations.art: A water strider skating towards an ant struggling on a pond, with rings of ripples spreading out from the ant and reaching the strider's legs.
explanations.context: This card is about water striders. It says what problem they solve by living on water, and how their legs help.

explanations.definition: A water strider moves by sweeping their middle legs backwards like oars. The legs push the water back, and the water pushes the strider forward.
explanations.description: Each middle leg presses a dent in the water's skin and sweeps it backwards fast. This pushes water backwards in small swirls. The water pushes back on the leg, so the strider shoots forward. The back legs steer, like a rudder. For a long time, some scientists thought striders moved mainly by making ripples. But baby water striders move their legs too slowly to make those ripples, and they still move well. In 2003, scientists in the United States added dye to the water and filmed striders at high speed. They saw the swirls pushed backwards, and showed that this is how striders move. They also built a little robot strider that rowed the same way.
examples: A water strider can move many times their own body length in one stroke.
Watch a strider in sunlight, and you may see the shadows of the dents move as they row.
explanations.art: Top view of a water strider sweeping their middle legs back, with small curled swirls drawn in the water behind each leg and an arrow showing the strider moving forward.
explanations.context: This card explains how a water strider moves across water, and how scientists found out.

explanations.concept: Other lives that use the water's skin
explanations.definition: Many small living things use the surface of water: some stand on it, some hang from it, and some use it to escape.
explanations.description: Mosquito larvae, the young of mosquitoes, live in still water. They hang just under the surface and breathe through a short tube that pokes through the skin. Health workers sometimes spread a thin film of special oil on stagnant water. The oil weakens the skin, so the larvae cannot hang on and breathe. Some small beetles, called rove beetles, live at the water's edge. If one falls in, they let out a soap-like liquid from their back end. It weakens the skin behind them, and the stronger skin in front pulls them forward fast. Some small water bugs escape in the same way, using their spit.
examples: Mosquito larvae hang under the surface of water left standing in a pot or a tyre.
Emptying standing water every week stops mosquitoes from growing there.
A rove beetle can shoot across water by letting out a soap-like liquid.
explanations.art: Under-water view of mosquito larvae hanging upside down from the surface, their breathing tubes poking through it, in a clay pot of water.
explanations.context: This card is about other small animals that live on or under the water's skin, like mosquito larvae.

explanations.concept: Is glass a very slow liquid?
explanations.description: Glass is made by melting sand and cooling it fast. Its particles stay in a jumble, like a liquid, instead of lining up in neat rows like a crystal. So people often ask if glass is a liquid that is too slow to see. Scientists agree that ordinary glass does not flow in any way we can measure at room temperature. They still argue about what exactly happens to the particles as a hot runny liquid turns into hard glass.
examples: Window glass hundreds of years old has not flowed in any way anyone can measure.
Hot glass in a glass factory flows like very thick honey.

perspectives.explanation: Glass is a solid. Its particles are jumbled like a liquid's, but they are stuck in place. At room temperature it would take far longer than people have existed to sag at all.
Glass is a liquid that has slowed down so much that it seems frozen. How a liquid slows into a glass is still one of the big unsolved puzzles of physics.

explanations.art: Two magnified circles side by side: neat rows of particles labelled crystal, and a jumble of particles labelled glass.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument among scientists: is glass a solid, or a very slow liquid?

agreed.text: Every liquid has a viscosity, and different liquids flow at very different speeds.
agreed.evidence: Scientists time liquids flowing through narrow tubes, and record their viscosity in tables. Anyone can see the difference by racing liquids down a slope.

agreed.text: Warming makes almost every liquid less viscous, so it flows faster.
agreed.evidence: Measurements of honey, oils and syrups at different temperatures all show this. Honey can flow ten times faster when it is warm.

agreed.text: Water has a strong surface tension, because water particles attract each other strongly. Soap makes it much weaker.
agreed.evidence: The pull of the surface can be measured with a ring or a plate pulled up from water. Agnes Pockels measured how soap and oil change it in her kitchen, in the 1880s.

agreed.text: Water striders stand on water because their waxy, hairy legs repel water, and surface tension holds up the small dents they make.
agreed.evidence: Scientists have looked at the legs under powerful microscopes and measured how much weight one leg can hold up. In 2004, a team in China found that one leg can hold about 15 times the insect's weight.

challenging.claim: Thick liquids are heavier than runny ones.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Honey is thick, and a jar of honey is heavier than the same jar of water.
challenging.against: Coconut oil is more viscous than water, but it is lighter. Pour it on water, and it floats. Thickness is about how a liquid flows, not how heavy it is.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up: thinking that thick means heavy.

challenging.claim: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom because the glass has slowly flowed down.
challenging.who: A story often told in books and by tour guides
challenging.for: Some very old window panes in Europe really are thicker at one edge.
challenging.against: Old glass was made by spinning hot glass into a disc, so panes came out uneven. Builders often put the thick edge at the bottom, but sometimes at the top or sides. Scientists have worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than people have existed to sag in any way we could see.
challenging.context: This card is about a popular story that says glass flows. The evidence says it does not, at room temperature.

challenging.claim: Pitch, which shatters under a hammer, is really a liquid.
challenging.who: Thomas Parnell, a physics professor in Australia, in 1927
challenging.for: Pitch has been dripping out of a funnel at the University of Queensland since 1930. Nine drops have fallen.
challenging.against: Pitch breaks into sharp pieces when hit, like a solid. Some people say it is fairer to call it a solid that flows.
challenging.context: This card is about pitch, which looks and breaks like a solid but drips like a liquid.

challenging.claim: A water strider stays up only because they are very light.
challenging.for: Water striders are small and light. A heavy insect, like a beetle, would sink.
challenging.against: Add a drop of soap to the water, and a water strider sinks, though their weight has not changed. Their waxy, hairy legs matter as much as their weight. The legs keep the water from wetting them, so the skin holds.
challenging.context: This card is about why a water strider does not sink. Being light is only part of the answer.

challenging.claim: Water striders move by making ripples that push them along.
challenging.for: A rowing strider does make ripples, and ripples carry energy.
challenging.against: Baby water striders move their legs too slowly to make those ripples, yet they move well. In 2003, filming showed that striders move mainly by pushing swirls of water backwards with their legs.
challenging.context: This card is about an idea scientists had about how striders move, and how it was tested.

big_questions.q: Pitch shatters like a solid but drips like a liquid. Is it a solid or a liquid? Who gets to decide?
big_questions.hint: Think about how long you watch. In one second, pitch acts like a solid. In ten years, it acts like a liquid.

big_questions.q: Honey is thick, and warm honey is runny. If the same honey can be both, is 'thick' really part of what honey is?
big_questions.hint: Remember the syrup race. What changed between the two spoons of honey, and what stayed the same?

big_questions.q: Water feels like nothing when you put your finger in it. Yet its skin holds up a living insect. What else might be stronger than it feels?
big_questions.hint: Think about the dome of water on the coin, and how many drops it took to break it.

big_questions.q: A water strider feels ripples with their legs and knows where food is. What would the world feel like if you lived on top of a pond?
big_questions.hint: Close your eyes and rest your fingertips on water while someone drops a grain of rice. What do you notice?

big_questions.q: If you could watch for a thousand years, which things around you would turn out to be flowing?
big_questions.hint: Think about glaciers, the rock under the Earth's crust, and the pitch drop.

big_questions.q: Why does warming make honey runny, but makes an egg go hard?
big_questions.hint: Honey's particles only move faster. In an egg, heat makes the particles join together in a new way.

story.title: The Skaters on Paati's Tank
story.note: Nila, her cousin Arjun, Paati and the town are made up. Water striders really do live on temple tanks and ponds across India, and soap really does make them sink.
text: Every May, Nila stayed with her Paati in a small town near Kumbakonam. Paati means grandmother in Tamil. Behind Paati's house was an old temple tank, a square pond with stone steps going down to the water on all four sides. Nila was nine. This year her cousin Arjun had come too. He was seven, and he had never seen a temple tank before.
On the first morning, Nila took Arjun down the steps to the water. It was early and still cool. The water was flat and green, and lotus leaves floated in one corner.
'Look,' said Nila, and she pointed. 'Skaters.'

Near the bottom step, a dozen thin brown insects stood on the water. They had long legs spread wide, like the legs of a stool. They did not swim. They stood on top of the water, as if it were a floor. Then one of them swept their middle legs back, and shot forward the length of Arjun's hand, and stopped.
Arjun crouched down. 'Why don't they fall in?'
'Look at their feet,' said Nila.
The sun was low and shone through the water onto the stone step below. Under each skater, on the stone, there were six little round shadows. They looked like dark coins with bright edges.
'Those are dents,' said Nila. 'Each foot pushes a small dent into the top of the water, like your finger pushing into a balloon. But the foot does not go through.'
'Why not?'
'Paati showed me last year. Come on.'

In the kitchen, Paati was making coffee. Nila took a one-rupee coin from the shelf and a steel tumbler of water. She dipped a straw into the water, put her finger over the top, and let drops fall onto the coin, one at a time. Arjun counted. At ten drops the water was a little hill. At twenty it was a tall shiny dome, higher than the edge of the coin. At twenty-six it spilled.
'See?' said Nila. 'The water holds on to itself. The top acts like a skin. Paati says scientists call it surface tension. The skaters stand on the skin.'
Paati smiled over her coffee. 'And their legs are covered in tiny hairs, with a kind of wax on them. Water cannot wet those legs. So the skin stays whole under their feet.'

For the next three days, Arjun went down to the tank every morning. He learned to sit very still on the bottom step. He saw that the skaters did not just stand about. When a small ant fell off a lotus leaf and kicked on the water, rings spread out around the ant. Within a moment, two skaters had turned and raced towards it. The first one grabbed the ant with their short front legs.
'They felt the ripples,' Arjun said at lunch. 'Like a phone buzzing.'

On the fourth morning, a man came down the far steps with a bucket and a bar of soap. He soaped his scooter's mudguards on the bottom step and splashed them clean. White foam slid across the water into the corner where the skaters were.

Nila and Arjun watched. One skater skated into the foam. Their feet slipped through. Their legs sank, and then their body tipped, and they were in the water, kicking and pulling, unable to climb back up.
'It's drowning,' said Arjun.
'They,' said Nila. 'Not it. And they're not drowning yet. Quick, get me a lotus leaf.'

Arjun pulled a small leaf from the edge. Nila slid it under the struggling skater and lifted them out. She carried the leaf to the other side of the tank, where the water was clear and calm, and tipped it gently. The skater sat still for a long moment. Then they rubbed their legs with their feet, one by one. Then they stepped onto the water, and stood, and skated away.
Arjun let out his breath. 'Why did the soap make them sink?'

That night, Nila showed him. She dropped water on the coin again, and Arjun counted to twenty-four before it spilled. Then she dried the coin and used water with one drop of soap stirred in. This time the water made a flat puddle, and spilled at eight.
'Soap breaks the skin,' said Nila. 'It makes the water hold on to itself less. Then the skaters' feet go through, and the water wets their legs.'
Arjun looked at the coin for a long time. 'So for us, soap is for washing. For them, it's like a hole in the floor.'

The next morning, Arjun pulled Nila across to the man with the scooter. Arjun was seven and very serious. He pointed at the corner, and at the skaters, and at the soap. Nila explained how soap breaks the water's skin. The man listened, scratched his head, and laughed. Then he carried his bucket up the steps and washed his scooter on the road instead.
story.epiphany: The top of water is a skin that holds itself together. Water striders live on that skin, and soap, which seems so harmless to us, breaks it under their feet.
ask: How could Nila and Arjun tell that each skater's foot made a dent in the water?
Why did the dome on the coin spill so much sooner when Nila added soap?
How did the skaters know where the fallen ant was?
Why did the skater rub their legs with their feet after Nila rescued them?
Arjun said soap is like a hole in the floor for a skater. Is that a good way to explain it? Why?

games.title: Runny or Thick? A guessing card game
games.context: This is a card game about kitchen liquids. You guess which of two liquids is thicker, and check with your own race results or a quick tip test.

printables.title: 16 liquid cards to cut out, each with a picture and a name
6 warmth cards: 3 'Warm it' and 3 'Chill it'
items: Warm it: this liquid has stood in warm water for 5 minutes
Chill it: this liquid has been in the fridge for an hour

printables.title: A score sheet with each player's name and boxes for points

rules: Shuffle the liquid cards and put them face down. Shuffle the warmth cards in a separate pile.
On your turn, turn over two liquid cards. Say which liquid is thicker, and why.
Check: use your syrup race or ladder results. If a liquid was not raced, tip a spoonful of each on a plate and watch.
Right guess: 1 point. A reason that uses the word 'particles' or 'viscosity': 1 more point.
Sometimes, turn over a warmth card too and put it on one liquid. Warmed liquids get runnier and chilled ones get thicker. Say how that changes your answer.
Playing alone, try to put all 16 cards in one line, from runniest to thickest.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the cards. 2. Make two piles, face down.
flow.say: Every card is a liquid from the kitchen. You will guess which of two is thicker.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Make two piles. Each card is a kitchen liquid.
flow.context: This is the start of Runny or Thick?, a card game where you guess which of two liquids is thicker.

flow.do: Play one practice round together with the honey and water cards.
flow.say: Practice round. Honey or water, which is thicker? Now put a 'Warm it' card on the honey. Which is thicker now?
flow.kid: Honey or water: which is thicker? Now the honey is warmed. Which is thicker now?

check.q: Honey has been warmed in warm water for 5 minutes. Is it now thicker or runnier than water?
options: Runnier than water
Still thicker than water, but runnier than before
Exactly as thick as water
check.why: Warming lowers honey's viscosity a lot, but warm honey is still far thicker than water. In the syrup race, warm honey beat cool honey but was still much slower than water. Picking 'runnier than water' goes too far.

flow.do: Take turns. Each turn, two cards, a guess and a reason. Check with your results.
flow.say: Turn over two cards. Which is thicker? Tell us why.
flow.kid: Turn two cards. Which is thicker? Say why. Then check.
flow.parent: Some pairs are close, such as milk and buttermilk. If the tip test does not show a clear winner, call it a draw. That is a good scientific answer.

flow.do: Count points, then ask the question below.
flow.say: Was any thick liquid also lighter than water? How could you check?
flow.kid: Count your points. Is any thick liquid lighter than water?
flow.think: How could you tell if a liquid is lighter than water? Hint: pour a little into a glass of water.
flow.parent: Oil, hair oil and melted ghee are thicker than water but float on it, so they are lighter.

setup.art: Two cards turned face up on a table, one showing a jar of honey and one a glass of milk, with a child pointing at the honey.
setup.caption: 1. Turn over two liquid cards. Which is thicker?

setup.art: A spoon of each liquid tipped onto a steel plate, one spreading fast and one slow.
setup.caption: 2. Check with your race results or a quick tip test.

games.title: Strider Hunt: a pond board game
games.context: This is a board game. Each player is a water strider on a temple tank. You skate to fallen insects, and watch out for fish, birds and soapy water.

printables.title: A pond board: a temple tank with 30 squares in a winding path across the water, steps at one side and lotus leaves
items: Start: the shady corner by the steps
Finish: the lotus leaves on the far side

printables.title: 18 pond cards to cut out
items: An ant falls in and struggles. You feel the ripples. Skate 3 squares to catch them.
A small fly lands on the water. Their kicks make tiny ripples. Skate 2 squares.
A moth falls in after a night of lights. Big ripples! Skate 4 squares.
You tap the water to send a ripple signal to another strider. Every player moves 1 square.
A fish rises under you. You feel the water bulge and jump away. Go back 1 square, but you are safe.
A kingfisher dives nearby. Stay very still: miss a turn.
Wind blows ripples across the whole tank. You cannot tell where food is. Miss a turn.
Soapy water runs in from someone washing at the steps. The skin is weak there. Go back 3 squares to clean water.
Oil from a scooter wash spreads on the water. Go back 2 squares.
You row hard with your middle legs and push the water back. Skate 3 squares.
Rain drops hit the water. Ripples everywhere! Miss a turn.
You clean your legs with your feet, to keep their waxy hairs dry. Stay where you are, but your next move is doubled.
A dragonfly lands on a lotus leaf. Not food for you. Stay where you are.
A baby water strider hatches nearby. Move 1 square to make room.
A leaf falls and makes a big dent. Skate around it: move 1 square.
A struggling ant reaches you. Grab them with your short front legs. Skate 2 squares.
The Sun warms the water. Skate 2 squares.
A child drops a stone into the tank. Big rings. Go back 1 square.

printables.title: 4 water strider tokens to cut out and fold, and a dice

rules: Each player puts a strider token on the Start corner.
On your turn, roll the dice and move that many squares across the water.
If you land on a square with a ripple drawn on it, take a pond card, read it aloud, and do what it says.
After each pond card, say why it helps or harms a water strider. A good reason earns a bonus square.
The first strider to reach the lotus leaves wins.
Playing alone, race against a second token that only moves when you roll a 5 or a 6.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the board pieces, cards and tokens. 2. Shuffle the pond cards. 3. Put the tokens on Start.
flow.say: You are water striders living on a temple tank. You hunt insects that fall onto the water. Let's see who reaches the lotus leaves first.
flow.kid: You are a water strider on a temple tank. Hunt for food. Reach the lotus leaves.
flow.context: This is the start of Strider Hunt, a board game about how water striders live on the surface of a pond.

flow.do: Play the soapy water card as a practice card.
flow.say: Practice card. Soapy water runs in from the steps. Why is that bad for a water strider?
flow.kid: Practice card: soapy water. Why is it bad for a water strider?

check.q: Soapy water runs into a pond. What happens to a water strider who skates into it?
options: Nothing, because water striders are very light
They sink, because soap weakens the water's skin and wets their legs
They go faster, like a soap boat
check.why: The strider stands on the water's skin, and their waxy hairs keep their legs dry. Soap weakens the skin and lets water wet the legs, so they sink. Picking 'very light' misses that the skin itself has changed. Picking 'faster' is a clever link to the soap boat, but the strider is standing in the soap, not in front of it.

flow.do: Take turns rolling and moving. Read each pond card aloud and say why it helps or harms.
flow.say: Roll, move, and read the card if you land on a ripple. Why does that help or harm a strider?
flow.kid: Roll and move. Read the card. Does it help or harm a strider? Why?
flow.parent: Help your child say what the strider needs: a strong water skin, dry legs, and clear ripples to find food.

flow.do: When someone wins, ask the question below.
flow.say: Which cards were about people? What could people do to keep a temple tank good for water striders?
flow.kid: Which cards were about people? How could people help striders?
flow.think: Where does the soapy water from our home go?
flow.parent: Good answers: do not wash clothes, vehicles or vessels with soap in ponds and tanks, and keep oil out of drains.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out the pond board and put the striders at the start.

experiments.title: The Syrup Race: which liquid is slowest, and does warmth change it?
experiments.context: In this experiment you race five kitchen liquids down a sloping tray and time each one. Then you race warm honey against honey at room warmth.
experiments.question: Which kitchen liquid flows slowest down a slope? And does the same honey flow faster when it is warm?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put water, coconut oil, shampoo and honey in order, from fastest to slowest. Then guess: will warm honey be faster, slower or the same as honey at room warmth? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Every liquid gets the same amount, half a level teaspoon, dropped on the same start line. Every lane is on the same tray, at the same slope, with the same finish line. Each lane is used once, so no liquid runs over another's track. In the honey race, the only thing that changes is how warm the honey is.

materials.item: a flat steel or plastic tray, or a big flat chopping board, about 30 centimetres long
books to make a stack about 8 centimetres high
a ruler and a little sticky tape, or a sketch pen to mark the tray's edges
water, coconut oil (or any cooking oil), shampoo, and honey
6 teaspoons, one for each liquid, so they do not mix
2 small steel bowls, and a big bowl of warm water, as warm as a bath
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
an old newspaper under the tray, and a damp cloth for wiping

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the warm water. It should feel comfortably warm on the inside of your wrist, like bath water, never hot from the stove. Do not taste the shampoo. Wash the tray with soap afterwards, and keep honey drips away from the floor, or ants will come.

schedule.what: Race water, oil, shampoo and honey down a sloping tray and time each. Then race warm honey against honey at room warmth.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Then draw the tray with each liquid's lane and how far it went.

flow.do: 1. Spread newspaper on the floor or table. 2. Put the tray on it. 3. Mark a start line 3 centimetres from the top edge, with tape on both sides. 4. Mark a finish line 15 centimetres below it. 5. Put the stack of books under the top end.
flow.say: This tray is our race track. Every liquid starts here and must reach the finish line down there.
flow.kid: Put tape on both edges at the top. That is the start line. Measure 15 centimetres down. Tape again. That is the finish line.
flow.parent: The marks only need to be on the two side edges. Your child can look across from one mark to the other. A slope of about 8 centimetres on a 30 centimetre tray works well. Too steep, and everything is too fast to time.
flow.context: This is the first step of the syrup race. You make a sloping race track from a tray and some books.

flow.do: 1. Show the four liquids. 2. Let your child tip each bottle slowly and look. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Look at how each one moves in its bottle. Which will be fastest down the tray? Which will be slowest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Tip each bottle slowly. Watch it move. Which will win? Which will come last? Why?

ask.q: Put them in order from fastest to slowest. What is your reason?
good: Water first, because it splashes and pours fast.
Honey last, because it is thick and sticky.
Oil before shampoo, because shampoo is thicker.

flow.parent: Write the guesses in the 'My guess' column. Any order with a reason is a good guess. Don't say what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Lay the tray flat for a moment. 2. Put half a level teaspoon of water on the start line, in the left lane. 3. Lift the top onto the books and start the stopwatch. 4. Stop it when the front of the liquid crosses the finish line. 5. Do the same for oil and shampoo, each in their own lane.
flow.say: Ready? I lift, you start the stopwatch. Stop it the moment the front of the liquid crosses the finish line.
flow.kid: Lift the tray onto the books. Start the stopwatch. Stop it at the finish line. Write the time.
flow.parent: Lift the tray onto the books smoothly, not with a bang. Water will probably finish in about one or two seconds, which is hard to time. Writing 'under 2 seconds' is fine. Oil often takes a few seconds, and shampoo much longer. If your coconut oil has gone white and hard in a cool room, stand the bottle in warm water first. If a liquid has not finished after 5 minutes, write how far it got with the ruler.
flow.context: This is the racing step of the syrup race. Each liquid gets its own lane, and you time how long it takes to reach the finish line.

flow.do: 1. Lay the tray flat again. 2. Put half a teaspoon of honey on the start line, in a new lane. 3. Lift, start the stopwatch, and watch until it crosses the line, or until 5 minutes have passed.
flow.say: Now the honey. Watch it carefully. How is it moving compared with the water?
flow.kid: Now the honey. Start the stopwatch. How is it moving? Wait for the finish line.
flow.parent: Honey at room warmth often takes one to four minutes to go 15 centimetres. It depends on your honey and your room. While you wait, ask your child what they notice about the front of the honey. It often stays round and fat.

flow.do: 1. Put half a teaspoon of honey in each small bowl. 2. Stand one bowl in the big bowl of warm water. 3. Leave the other on the table. 4. Wait 5 minutes.
flow.say: Both bowls have the same honey. One sits in warm water and one stays on the table. Will the warm honey be faster, slower, or the same? Why?
flow.kid: Same honey in two bowls. One sits in warm water. Will warm honey be faster? Why do you think so?
flow.wait: Wait 5 minutes while the honey warms. Look back at the table of results.

ask.q: What do you think the warmth will do, and why?
good: Faster, because warm things melt and get runny.
Slower, because warm honey is stickier.
The same, because it is still honey.

flow.parent: Any guess with a reason is good. A grown-up mixes the warm water from the tap or a kettle with some cold water. It should feel like bath water.

flow.do: 1. Lay the tray flat. 2. Scoop the warm honey onto the start line in a new lane. 3. At the same moment, put the room-warm honey in the next lane. 4. Lift the tray and start the stopwatch. 5. Time each one to the finish line.
flow.say: Two honeys, side by side. Lift, start, and watch which one wins.
flow.kid: Put both honeys on the start line together. Lift the tray. Which one wins?

check.q: The warm honey ran down much faster than the honey at room warmth. Why?
options: The warm water got mixed into the honey
Warmth made the honey's particles move faster, so they slipped past each other more easily
The warm honey was heavier
check.why: The honey stayed in its own bowl, so no water got in. Warmth makes the particles in a liquid jiggle harder, so they let go of each other more easily and slide past. So the honey flows faster. Picking 'water got mixed in' is a good thought, so check: was the bowl dry inside? Picking 'heavier' mixes up thick and heavy, but the amount of honey was the same.

flow.parent: Warm honey usually runs several times faster. If your tray has no clean lanes left, wipe two lanes with a damp cloth and dry them well. If the difference is small, the warm water may have cooled. Make it warm again and try once more.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the 'Real place' column. 2. Compare it with the guesses. 3. Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Was your guess right? Now tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? And why did it happen?
flow.kid: Fill in the real places. Was your guess right? Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: honey has the highest viscosity, and warmth lowers it. What I saw: water finished in about a second and honey took minutes. Warm honey beat the same honey at room warmth. Why: honey's particles cling together and slide slowly, and warmth helps them slip past each other.
flow.think: If you put the honey in the fridge for an hour, what do you think would happen in the race?

experiments.title: How Many Drops Fit on a Coin?
experiments.context: In this experiment you add drops of water to a coin, one by one, and count how many fit before the water spills. Then you try soapy water and oil.
experiments.question: How many drops of water can sit on a coin before they spill? Does soapy water or oil hold as many?
experiments.predict: Guess first. How many drops of plain water will fit on a one-rupee coin before it spills? Will soapy water fit more drops, fewer, or the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: The same coin is used every time, wiped clean and dry between tries. The drops are all made the same way, with the same dropper or straw, from the same height. Each liquid is tried three times, because one try can be a fluke.

materials.item: a one-rupee coin, or any coin
a medicine dropper, or a drinking straw to use as a dropper
3 small cups: plain water, water with 3 drops of dish soap stirred in, and cooking oil
a steel plate to put the coin on, a tissue or cloth to dry the coin
paper and pencil to tally the drops

experiments.safety: None needed. Wipe up oil spills so nobody slips.

schedule.what: Count how many drops of water, soapy water and oil fit on a coin before they spill. Try each one three times.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the coin from the side, with the water dome just before it spilled.

flow.do: 1. Put the dry coin on the steel plate. 2. Show how to use the dropper. With a straw, dip it in water, press a finger on the top end, and lift. Lift the finger a little to let one drop fall.
flow.say: We will drop water onto this coin, one drop at a time. We count every drop until the water spills over the edge.
flow.kid: Put the coin on the plate. Practise making one drop at a time.
flow.parent: A straw dropper takes a little practice. Let your child make a few drops on the plate first. Hold the dropper just above the coin, about one centimetre, and let each drop fall gently.
flow.context: This is the first step of the coin drop experiment. You learn to make one drop at a time.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: How many drops of water do you think will fit on the coin? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How many drops will fit before it spills? Why?

ask.q: How many drops will fit, and why?
good: Three, because the coin is small and flat.
Ten, because drops are small.
Lots, because the water can pile up.

flow.parent: Most children guess between 2 and 10. Write the guess down.

flow.do: 1. Drop plain water onto the middle of the coin, one drop at a time. 2. Make a tally mark for every drop. 3. Stop when the water spills over the edge. 4. Dry the coin and repeat twice more.
flow.say: Count out loud. Look at the coin from the side. What shape is the water making?
flow.kid: Drop, count, drop, count. Look from the side. What shape is the water?

ask.q: What do you notice about the water as you add drops?
good: It makes a hill.
It goes higher than the edge of the coin.
It wobbles but does not spill.

flow.parent: A one-rupee coin usually holds somewhere between 15 and 40 drops, depending on the coin and the drop size. The water makes a dome that rises well above the edge. That surprises most children.

flow.do: 1. Dry the coin well. 2. Do the same with the soapy water, three times. 3. Then do it with the oil, three times, wiping the coin with a tissue between tries.
flow.say: Now soapy water. Will it make the same tall dome? Then oil.
flow.kid: Now try soapy water three times. Then oil three times. Count each drop.
flow.parent: Soapy water usually holds far fewer drops, and makes a low, flat puddle that spills early. Oil also spreads flatter than water. Dry the coin very well after the soapy water. Any soap left on it will spoil the next plain water try.

flow.do: 1. For each liquid, put the three numbers in order. 2. Circle the middle one. 3. Write it in the 'Middle number' column.
flow.say: Put your three numbers in order, and pick the middle one. That is a fair number for each liquid.
flow.kid: Put the three numbers in order. Circle the middle one.

check.q: Plain water made a tall dome on the coin. Soapy water spilled after far fewer drops. Why?
options: Soap makes water heavier
Soap weakens the pull between water particles at the surface, so the skin breaks sooner
The soapy water was colder
check.why: Water particles attract each other. At the surface this pull acts like a stretchy skin that holds the dome up. Soap gets between the water particles at the surface and makes the skin much weaker. Picking 'heavier' is a common guess, but three drops of soap hardly change the weight. Picking 'colder' is a careful thought, but both cups were in the same room.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see? Why did it happen?
flow.kid: Say what you think, what you saw, and why.
flow.parent: A good answer sounds like this. What I think: water has a strong skin, and soap makes it weaker. What I saw: water piled up to 28 drops in a tall dome, soapy water spilled at 9. Why: water particles pull on each other at the surface, and soap gets in the way.
flow.think: A water strider stands on the water's skin. What do you think would happen to a strider if soapy water ran into their pond?

activities.title: Pour and Watch: water and honey
activities.context: This is a quick start to the unit. You pour water and honey from spoons and watch how differently they move.

materials.item: a steel plate, two teaspoons, a little water and a little honey

activities.safety: None needed. Wipe up honey drips.

schedule.what: Pour water and honey from spoons onto a plate. Say what you notice, and wonder why.

activities.record: Draw the water stream and the honey stream side by side.

flow.do: 1. Fill one spoon with water and one with honey. 2. Hold both about 10 centimetres above the plate. 3. Tip them at the same moment.
flow.say: Watch both spoons. Tell me everything you notice.
flow.kid: Tip both spoons at the same time. Watch closely. What do you notice?

ask.q: What do you notice? What do you wonder?
good: The water fell fast and splashed.
The honey made a long thread.
The honey piled up in loops like a rope.
Why is honey so slow?

flow.context: This is the opening activity of the unit. You watch water and honey pour from spoons.

flow.do: Pour the honey again, very slowly, from higher up, and watch where it lands.
flow.say: Look where the honey lands. What is it doing on the plate?
flow.kid: Pour the honey again, slowly. Watch it land. What shape does it make?
flow.parent: A thin stream of honey often coils into loops as it lands, like a rope being laid down. Water never does this.

flow.do: Ask why the two are so different, and listen to the whole answer.
flow.say: Both are liquids. Why do you think the honey is so slow?
flow.kid: Water and honey are both liquids. Why is honey so slow? What do you think?
flow.parent: Common answers are 'honey is heavy', 'honey is sticky' and 'honey is thick'. Don't correct them yet. The syrup race will test some of them.
flow.think: How could you find out which of your kitchen liquids is the slowest of all?

setup.art: Two spoons tipped together over a steel plate, water splashing down fast, honey hanging in a long thread.
setup.caption: 1. Tip both spoons at the same moment.

setup.art: A thin honey stream landing on a plate and coiling into neat loops, like a rope.
setup.caption: 2. Pour the honey slowly and watch it coil.

activities.title: The Thread Loop: watch soap break the water's skin
activities.context: In this activity you float a loop of thread on water, then touch soap inside it and watch what happens.

materials.item: a big steel plate or thali, filled with clean water
a piece of cotton sewing thread about 20 centimetres long, tied into a loop
a toothpick or a matchstick, and a drop of dish soap or liquid hand soap

schedule.what: Float a loop of thread on water. Touch soap inside the loop and watch it change shape.

activities.record: Draw the loop before and after the soap touched it.

flow.do: 1. Let the water in the plate go completely still. 2. Lay the thread loop gently on the water, so it floats in a wiggly shape.
flow.say: Lay the loop on the water very gently. Look at its shape.
flow.kid: Lay the thread loop on the water gently. What shape is it?
flow.parent: The plate must be rinsed well, with no soap left on it. If the thread sinks, lay it down more gently, or try a thinner thread.
flow.context: This is the first step of the thread loop activity. You float a loop of thread on still water.

flow.do: Dip the tip of the toothpick in soap. Ask for a guess before it touches the water.
flow.say: I will touch soap to the water inside the loop. What will the thread do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Soap will touch the water inside the loop. What will the thread do?

ask.q: What will happen to the loop, and why?
good: It will sink, because soap is heavy.
It will move away from the soap.
Nothing, because soap is only a little.

flow.do: Touch the soapy tip to the water in the middle of the loop, and hold it still.
flow.say: Watch the thread!
flow.kid: Touch the soap inside the loop. Watch the thread!

check.q: The wiggly loop snapped into a round circle. Why?
options: The soap pushed the thread outwards
The soap weakened the skin inside the loop, so the stronger skin outside pulled the thread outwards
The thread got wet and heavy
check.why: The water's skin pulls on the thread from both sides. Soap makes the skin inside the loop weaker. The stronger skin outside pulls the thread out evenly in every direction, so it makes a circle. Picking 'soap pushed' is a fair guess, but the soap never touched the thread. Picking 'wet and heavy' would make it sink, not make a circle.

flow.parent: The loop jumps into a circle in less than a second. It is quick, so watch closely.

flow.do: Rinse the plate well, fill it with fresh water, and try again with a new loop.
flow.say: Let's do it again. Why do we need fresh water each time?
flow.kid: Rinse the plate. Use fresh water. Try it again.
flow.parent: Soap spreads over the whole water, so a second try in the same water does not work. This is a good thing to talk about: a little soap changes the whole surface.

setup.art: A wiggly loop of white thread floating on water in a steel thali.
setup.caption: 1. Float a loop of thread on still water.

setup.art: A soapy toothpick touching the water inside the loop, and the loop now a perfect circle.
setup.caption: 2. Touch soap inside the loop. The loop becomes a circle.

activities.title: The Ripple Hunter: find food like a water strider
activities.context: In this activity you find out how a water strider knows where food is. You watch, then feel, ripples spreading on water.

materials.item: a big steel plate or a wide basin of water
a few tiny squares of paper, about 1 centimetre wide
a spoon, and a few grains of rice

schedule.what: Watch ripples spread and make paper squares bob. Then, with eyes closed, feel where a ripple comes from.

activities.record: Draw the basin from above, with the ripple rings and the paper squares.

flow.do: 1. Let the water go still. 2. Float the paper squares near one edge. 3. Drop one grain of rice onto the far side.
flow.say: Watch the water, and watch the paper squares.
flow.kid: Float the paper squares. Drop a rice grain on the far side. Watch.

ask.q: What happened to the paper squares?
good: Rings spread out from the rice.
The papers bobbed when the rings reached them.

flow.context: This is the first step of the ripple hunter activity. You watch ripples spread across water from a falling rice grain.

flow.do: Explain how a water strider hunts.
flow.say: A water strider hunts insects that fall onto ponds. A fallen ant kicks and struggles. That sends out rings like these. The strider feels the rings through their legs, and turns towards them.
flow.kid: A water strider feels ripples with their legs. That is how they find food.

flow.do: 1. Your child closes their eyes. 2. They rest four fingertips very lightly on the water, as if they had strider legs. 3. Drop a rice grain or one drop of water on one side. 4. They point to where it came from.
flow.say: Close your eyes. Rest your fingertips on the water, very lightly. When you feel a ripple, point to where it came from.
flow.kid: Close your eyes. Touch the water lightly with your fingertips. Point where the ripple came from.
flow.parent: Keep the room quiet and the fingertips still. Many children can feel the ripple arrive. If your child cannot, they can open their eyes and watch the paper squares instead.
flow.think: A water strider has six legs spread wide. How could that help them tell which way a ripple came from?

setup.caption: 1. Drop a rice grain and watch the rings reach the paper.

setup.art: A child with eyes closed resting four fingertips lightly on the water, pointing with the other hand towards where a ripple came from.

activities.title: The Bubble Race: flip the bottles
activities.context: In this activity you turn closed bottles of different liquids upside down, and time how long the air bubble takes to rise. It is another way to compare how thick liquids are.

materials.item: clear closed bottles with a little air at the top: a water bottle, a clear bottle of coconut oil or cooking oil, and a clear bottle or jar of honey
a phone stopwatch

activities.safety: Check every cap is screwed on tight before flipping.

schedule.what: Flip three bottles and time how long the air bubble takes to rise to the top.

activities.record: Write each bottle's bubble time in a small table.

flow.do: 1. Check the caps are tight. 2. Stand the bottles in a row. 3. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: When we turn each bottle upside down, the air bubble will rise. In which bottle will it rise slowest? Why?
flow.kid: Flip each bottle. The bubble will rise. Which bubble will be slowest? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the bubble race. You guess which bottle's air bubble will rise slowest.

flow.do: 1. Flip one bottle and start the stopwatch. 2. Stop it when the last of the air reaches the top. 3. Do the same for each bottle.
flow.say: Flip it, start the clock. Stop when the air is all at the top.
flow.kid: Flip the bottle. Start the clock. Stop when the bubble reaches the top.
flow.parent: In water, the bubble rises in about a second. In oil, it takes a few seconds. In honey, it can take a minute or more. Bottles of different sizes give different times, so the honey result is a rough comparison, not a perfectly fair test.

flow.do: Compare with the syrup race results.
flow.say: Did the bubble race put the liquids in the same order as the syrup race?
flow.kid: Is the order the same as in the syrup race?

ask.q: Why did the bubble rise so slowly in the honey?
good: The honey is very viscous, so it moves out of the bubble's way slowly.
The honey's particles cling together.

activities.title: Ketchup and Curd: thinner when stirred
activities.context: In this activity you find two foods that get runnier when you shake or stir them.

materials.item: a bottle of tomato ketchup with some ketchup in it
a small bowl of set curd, and a spoon
a plate

activities.safety: None needed. The curd can be eaten afterwards.

schedule.what: Turn ketchup upside down, then tap it. Tip set curd, then stir it and tip it again.

activities.record: Write two sentences: what the ketchup did, and what the curd did.

flow.do: 1. Hold the ketchup bottle upside down over the plate, without squeezing or shaking. 2. Count to ten. 3. Now tap the bottom of the bottle firmly with your palm.
flow.say: Upside down, and no squeezing. Does it come out? Now tap it hard.
flow.kid: Hold the ketchup upside down. Don't squeeze. Wait. Now tap it hard.

ask.q: What did the ketchup do when you tapped it?
good: It suddenly came out.
It stayed still, then ran.

flow.context: This is the first step of the ketchup and curd activity. You find out what tapping does to ketchup.

flow.do: 1. Tilt the bowl of set curd slowly and see if it slides. 2. Stir it hard with a spoon for 30 seconds. 3. Tilt it again.
flow.say: Tilt the curd. Does it slide? Now stir it hard and tilt it again. What changed?
flow.kid: Tilt the curd bowl. Now stir it hard. Tilt it again. What changed?
flow.parent: Set curd holds its shape. After stirring it is much runnier and flows in the bowl. Leave it for an hour, and it gets only a little thicker again.

flow.do: Talk about why.
flow.say: Ketchup and curd have tiny bits inside them that hold each other in a loose net. Shaking and stirring break the net, so they flow.
flow.kid: Shaking breaks a tiny net inside ketchup and curd. Then they flow.

check.q: Anjali, a girl in Class 3, cannot get ketchup out of a full bottle. What should she try?
options: Put the bottle in the fridge
Tap or shake the bottle
Hold it still for longer
check.why: Tapping or shaking breaks the tiny net inside the ketchup, so it becomes runnier and flows. Cold makes most liquids thicker, so the fridge would make it worse. Holding it still lets the net stay in place.

projects.title: The Kitchen Thickness Ladder: race the foods you eat
projects.context: This 3-day project uses the syrup race tray to test the liquids in your kitchen. At the end you make a ladder chart, from runniest to thickest.

materials.item: the race tray, books and stopwatch from the syrup race

a long strip of paper and colour pencils for the ladder chart

schedule.what: Race four kitchen liquids down the tray and time each one.
Race four more liquids. Add the syrup race times too.
Make the ladder chart, runniest at the top and thickest at the bottom, and explain it to the family.

projects.record: A ladder chart on a long strip of paper, with each liquid's name, picture and time on its own rung.

flow.do: 1. Set up the tray as in the syrup race. 2. Pick four kitchen liquids. 3. Guess their order. 4. Race each one with half a teaspoon, and time it.
flow.say: Which of these is the runniest, do you think? Which is the thickest? Let's race them and see.
flow.kid: Pick four kitchen liquids. Guess their order. Race them and time each one.
flow.parent: Use only half a teaspoon of each, so little food is wasted. The tray must be the same slope every day, so keep the same books.

flow.do: Race four more liquids on day 2, the same way.
flow.say: Same tray, same books, same spoon. Why must everything stay the same as yesterday?
flow.kid: Race four more. Keep everything the same as yesterday. Why?
flow.parent: A good answer: so the times from both days can be compared fairly.

flow.do: 1. Draw a ladder on a long strip of paper. 2. Put the fastest liquid on the top rung, and the slowest at the bottom. 3. Your child explains the ladder to the family.
flow.say: Put the fastest at the top and the slowest at the bottom. Then tell everyone what you found.
flow.kid: Draw a ladder. Fastest at the top. Slowest at the bottom. Explain it to your family.
flow.think: Which liquids surprised you? Was any thick liquid lighter than water?

challenges.title: Slow Down the Water
challenges.context: This is a challenge. You turn plain water into a liquid as slow as honey, using only things from the kitchen.
challenges.problem: Lakshmi Aunty runs a small juice stall in Mysuru. She wants to make a thick drink that pours as slowly as honey. Start with 4 spoons of water. Add things from the kitchen to make it race down the tray as slowly as your honey did.
constraints: Use only things from the kitchen, cold, with no cooking.
Test it on the syrup race tray, at the same slope.
materials: water, a small cup and teaspoons
sugar, atta, rice flour or besan
the syrup race tray, books and stopwatch
general: Stir in sugar, spoon by spoon. Lots of sugar makes a thick syrup, but it takes a lot.
Stir in atta or rice flour, a little at a time, to make a batter. This is how dosa batter gets thick.
Stir in besan. It thickens water quickly.
creative: Mix two thickeners, such as sugar and atta.
Leave the mixture to stand for 10 minutes, then stir and test again.
Use the cold, leftover water from boiled rice, called kanji, if your family has some.
challenges.your_turn: Now try your own idea. Write down exactly what you added, so someone else could make the same liquid.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud and set out the thickeners.
flow.say: We want water to be as slow as honey. What could we add to it? Why do you think it would work?
flow.kid: Make water as slow as honey. What could you add? Why?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Slow Down the Water challenge. You plan how to thicken water.

flow.do: 1. Try one thickener at a time. 2. After each spoon, race half a teaspoon down the tray. 3. Write down what you added and the time.
flow.say: Add one spoon, then test. Is it slower now?
flow.kid: Add one spoon. Stir well. Race it. Is it slower?
flow.parent: Flour batters thicken fast. Sugar needs many spoons. Keep a list, because the best mixture is only useful if you can make it again.

flow.do: Compare the best mixture's time with the honey's time.
flow.say: Which mixture came closest to honey? What did you add, and why do you think it worked?
flow.kid: Which mixture was closest to honey? Why did it work?
flow.think: Flour particles are long and big. How might that slow the water down?

challenges.title: The Soap Boat: move a boat without touching it
challenges.context: This is a challenge. You make a small card boat move across water using only a drop of soap.
challenges.problem: Design a small boat that moves across a basin of water on its own, with no pushing, blowing or touching. You may use one drop of soap each time.
constraints: The boat must be made from card or paper.
No pushing, blowing or touching the boat after it is placed.
Use fresh water for every try.
materials: a big basin or bucket of clean water
thin card, such as an old visiting card or cereal box
dish soap or liquid hand soap, and a toothpick
general: Cut a boat shape about 3 centimetres long, with a small notch cut into the back.
Put the boat on the water and touch a soapy toothpick into the notch.
The soap weakens the skin behind the boat, and the stronger skin in front pulls it forward.
creative: Make the notch on one side, so the boat turns in circles.
Try different shapes: long and thin, round, or a triangle.
Race two boats in two basins.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own boat. Draw it, test it, and measure how far it goes.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Remind your child about the thread loop.
flow.say: Remember the thread loop that jumped into a circle? Soap weakens the water's skin. How could that move a boat?
flow.kid: Soap makes the water's skin weaker. How could that move a boat?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Soap Boat challenge. You plan a boat that soap can move.

flow.do: 1. Cut a boat with a notch at the back. 2. Put it on the water at one end. 3. Touch a soapy toothpick into the notch. 4. Measure how far it goes. 5. Change the water and try a new design.
flow.say: Touch the soap into the notch. Watch the boat!
flow.kid: Put soap in the notch. Watch it go! Measure how far.
flow.parent: A grown-up helps with the scissors. The boat zooms forward for a few seconds, then stops when the soap has spread over the water. Soap left in the water stops the next try, so empty and refill the basin each time.

check.q: Why does the boat move forward when soap touches the back?
options: The soap pushes the boat like a motor
Soap weakens the water's skin behind the boat, so the stronger skin in front pulls it forward
The soap makes the boat lighter
check.why: The water's skin pulls the boat from every side. Soap weakens the pull behind it, so the pull in front wins. Some rove beetles escape across water in the same way, by letting out a soap-like liquid. Picking 'motor' is how it looks, but the soap only weakens the skin.

flow.do: Compare designs.
flow.say: Which boat went furthest? Why do you think it worked best?
flow.kid: Which boat went furthest? Why?
flow.think: If soapy water from a washing step ran into a pond, what would happen to the water striders?
