opts: How much a liquid resists flowing
quiz.why: Viscosity is how much a liquid resists flowing. Picking 'heavy' mixes up thick and heavy, and coconut oil shows they are different: thicker than water, but it floats.

quiz.p: Which of these has the highest viscosity?
quiz.why: Honey flows slowest, so it has the highest viscosity. Water and rasam are runny.

quiz.p: Kavya races half a teaspoon of each liquid down a tray. Why must every liquid use the same amount?
opts: So the test is fair, and only the liquid changes
quiz.why: In a fair test only one thing changes. A bigger blob can flow differently, so the amounts must be the same.

quiz.p: In the syrup race, water took about 1 second and honey took about 150 seconds. What does that tell you?
opts: Honey is much more viscous than water
quiz.why: The longer a liquid takes to flow, the higher its viscosity. Honey took far longer.

quiz.p: Why does warm honey flow faster than cool honey?
opts: Warm honey has water in it
Warmth makes honey's particles move faster, so they slip past each other more easily
quiz.why: Warmth makes the particles jiggle harder, so they let go of their neighbours more easily. Picking 'water in it' is a fair worry, but the honey was in its own dry bowl.

quiz.p: Ghee is thick on a cool morning. What will make it pour easily?
quiz.why: Warming lowers viscosity, so the ghee flows. Cold makes it thicker.

quiz.p: Why can a coin hold a dome of water higher than its edge?
opts: Water particles attract each other, so the surface acts like a stretchy skin
quiz.why: This is surface tension. The pull between water particles at the surface holds the dome together. The coin's metal has nothing to do with it.

quiz.p: What does soap do to the water's skin?
quiz.why: Soap weakens the skin. That is why the soapy dome spilled sooner and the thread loop jumped into a circle.

quiz.p: A water strider hunts insects that fall onto ponds. How do they find a fallen ant?
opts: They smell the ant from far away
They feel the ant's ripples through their legs
They wait for the ant to swim to them
quiz.why: A struggling ant sends out ripples. The strider feels them through their legs and skates towards them.

quiz.p: Soapy water runs into a pond. What happens to the water striders there?
opts: They sink, because the skin weakens and their legs get wet
quiz.why: The striders need a strong skin and dry legs. Soap takes away both, so they break through and sink.

quiz.p: In the pitch drop experiment, what did the dripping funnel show?
opts: Pitch is a liquid that flows extremely slowly
quiz.why: Pitch feels hard and shatters when hit, but it has dripped out of the funnel since 1930. It flows, only extremely slowly.

quiz.p: Pitch shatters under a hammer, but drips over many years. What does this show about solids and liquids?
opts: They are always easy to tell apart
Whether something acts solid or liquid can depend on how long you watch it
Pitch is a special kind of gas
quiz.why: Hit fast, pitch breaks like a solid. Over years, it flows like a liquid. The time you watch for decides what you see.

worksheets.title: Thick, Runny and the Water's Skin (core)

items.p: What does viscosity mean?
opts: How much a liquid resists flowing
items.why: Viscosity is how much a liquid resists flowing. Honey has a high viscosity and flows slowly. Picking 'heavy' is the most common mix-up: thick and heavy are different things.

items.p: Kavya puts half a teaspoon each of water, honey and shampoo at the top of a sloping tray. Which reaches the bottom first?
items.why: Water has the lowest viscosity of the three, so it flows fastest. Shampoo is slower, and honey is slowest.

items.p: In the syrup race, warm honey raced the same honey at room warmth. What happened?
opts: The honey at room warmth was faster
items.why: Warmth makes the honey's particles move faster, so they slip past each other more easily, and the honey flows faster.

items.p: Plain water made a tall dome on a coin. Then Priya tried water with a drop of soap. What did she see?
opts: A flatter puddle that spilled sooner
items.why: Soap weakens the water's skin, so it cannot hold up a tall dome. It spills after fewer drops.

items.p: How do a water strider's legs help them stand on water?
opts: Their legs are full of air like balloons
Their legs have tiny waxy hairs that keep water off, so the water's skin holds
Their legs are sticky, so they hold on to the water
items.why: The hairs and wax keep the legs dry, so each foot only dents the water's skin and does not break through.

items.p: A thick liquid is always heavier than a runny liquid.
items.why: False. Coconut oil is thicker than water, but lighter, so it floats on water.

items.p: Every liquid can flow, even a very thick one.
items.why: True. Thick liquids flow slowly, but they do flow. Even pitch, which feels hard, drips.

items.p: Soap makes the skin on water stronger.
items.why: False. Soap makes the skin weaker. That is why the dome on the coin spilled sooner, and why the thread loop jumped into a circle.

items.p: How easily a liquid flows is called its ____.
items.why: Viscosity is the scientist's word for how thick or runny a liquid is.

items.p: The pull between particles at the top of water makes a skin. This is called surface ____.
items.why: Surface tension makes the top of water act like a stretchy skin.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: the top layer, where water meets the air
an insect who lives on top of ponds
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: Sort these kitchen liquids. Is each one runny or thick?
items.why: Runny liquids pour fast and splash. Thick ones pour slowly and pile up.

items.p: Why does warm honey run faster than cool honey? Use the word 'particles'.
items.a: Warmth makes the honey's particles jiggle harder, so they let go of each other and slip past each other more easily.
items.why: A strong answer says that the particles move faster when warm, and that this lets them slide past each other.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, says water striders stand on water only because they are light. What would you tell her?
items.a: Being light helps, but their legs matter too. Their waxy, hairy legs keep the water off, so the water's skin holds them. With soap in the water, they sink, though they are just as light.
items.why: A strong answer agrees that light weight helps, and adds the legs and the water's skin, with the soap evidence.

items.p: Draw the coin from the side, just before the water spilled. Show how high the water rose above the coin's edge.
items.a: A coin with a rounded dome of water rising clearly above its edge.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the water higher than the coin's edge, held up by its skin.
items.art: A coin seen from the side, with an empty space above it to draw on.

items.p: Meenakshi flips closed bottles of water, oil and honey upside down. In which one does the air bubble rise slowest?
items.why: Honey is the most viscous, so it moves out of the bubble's way very slowly.

items.p: A loop of thread floats on water. Soap touches the water inside the loop. What happens to the loop?
opts: It snaps into a round circle
It shrinks into a tiny knot
items.why: Soap weakens the skin inside the loop. The stronger skin outside pulls the thread outwards evenly, so it becomes a circle.

items.p: Zoya cannot get ketchup out of the bottle. She taps the bottle hard, and it runs out. Why?
opts: Tapping breaks a tiny net inside the ketchup, so it becomes runnier
Tapping adds air that pushes it out
items.why: Ketchup has tiny bits that hold each other in a loose net. Tapping breaks the net, and the ketchup flows.

items.p: Honey is left in the fridge for an hour, then raced down the tray. What do you predict?
opts: It will be slower than honey at room warmth
It will be faster than honey at room warmth
It will be as fast as water
items.why: Cold makes the honey's particles move more slowly, so they slide past each other less easily. The honey becomes even more viscous.

items.p: Put these in order, from the fastest down the tray to the slowest.
items.why: This is the usual order in the syrup race. Water has the lowest viscosity and honey the highest.

items.p: Coconut oil is thicker than water, yet it floats on water.
items.why: True. Coconut oil is more viscous than water but lighter, so it floats. Thick does not mean heavy.

items.p: Old window glass is thicker at the bottom because the glass has flowed down.
items.why: False. Old glass was made uneven, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Glass at room temperature does not flow in any way we can measure.

items.p: Warming makes most liquids ____, so they flow faster.
items.why: Warmth lowers viscosity, as the warm honey in the syrup race showed.

items.p: Match each liquid to the reason it is thick.
pairs: big sugar particles cling to water particles
long starch particles from the rice
tiny bits hold each other in a loose net
items.why: Each liquid is thick for its own reason, but in every case the particles find it hard to slide past each other.

items.p: Sort these. Does each one help a water strider or harm them?
items: an oil film from a scooter wash
items.why: Striders need a strong water skin, dry legs and clear ripples. Soap and oil weaken the skin, and rain hides the ripples from food.

items.p: Sana raced water using a full spoon and honey using half a spoon. She says honey is slower. Why is her test not fair? How would you fix it?
items.a: She used different amounts. A bigger blob may flow differently. She should use half a spoon of each, on the same slope.
items.why: A strong answer names the one thing that was different (the amount) and says to keep it the same for every liquid.

items.p: Think about the coin test. Why did the water dome spill sooner when there was soap in the water?
items.a: Water particles at the surface attract each other and make a skin that holds the dome up. Soap gets between them and weakens the skin, so it breaks after fewer drops.
items.why: A strong answer talks about the pull between water particles, and says that soap weakens it.

items.p: Pitch shatters when hit with a hammer. But in a funnel it has dripped nine drops since 1930. Three people talk about it.

views.who: Thomas Parnell, the physics professor who set up the funnel in 1927
views.says: Pitch is a liquid. It flows, only very slowly. Wait long enough and you will see it drip.

views.who: Revathi, a road builder who uses tar every day
views.says: Pitch is a solid. You can stand on it and break it into pieces. Something you can shatter is not a liquid.
It is both. In one second it acts like a solid. In ten years it acts like a liquid. It depends on how long you watch.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most, and why? Then say what one of the other views gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason, for example Kavya's, because the same pitch breaks when hit fast and drips over years. It also says what another view gets right, for example that Revathi is right that pitch acts like a solid in everyday life.
items.why: Each view has a point. Parnell's funnel shows pitch flows, Revathi's experience shows it acts solid when hit, and Kavya notices that time decides which you see.

items.p: Draw a water strider standing on water, seen from the side. Show the dents their feet make in the water's skin.
items.a: An insect with long legs, each foot pressing a small curved dip into the surface without breaking through.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the surface bending down under each foot but not broken.
items.art: A flat line across the page for the water's surface.

items.p: Health workers sometimes spread a thin film of special oil on stagnant water to stop mosquitoes. How does this work?
items.a: Mosquito larvae hang from the water's skin to breathe through a small tube. The oil weakens the skin, so they cannot hang on and breathe.
items.why: A strong answer links the oil to a weaker water skin, and the weaker skin to the larvae not being able to breathe.

items.p: Farhan raced water and oil. Strangely, the oil won. Which is the most likely reason?
opts: His tray was tipped more steeply in the oil's lane, or the water spread out sideways
items.why: Usually water is faster. When a result is odd, check the test before changing the idea. A tilted tray or water spreading sideways can change the result.

items.p: A halwai warms thick jaggery syrup before pouring it into moulds. Why?
opts: Warm syrup is runnier, so it pours easily
Warm syrup is lighter, so it floats
items.why: Warming lowers the syrup's viscosity, just like the warm honey in the syrup race.

items.p: Baby water striders move their legs too slowly to make proper ripples, yet they still move well. What did this tell scientists?
opts: Striders must move in some other way than by making ripples
items.why: If babies move without making those ripples, ripples cannot be the main way striders move. In 2003, filming showed they push swirls of water backwards with their legs.

items.p: Which test shows best that thick does not mean heavy?
opts: Pour coconut oil onto water and see if it floats
items.why: Coconut oil is thicker than water. If it floats, it is lighter than water. So a liquid can be thick and light.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair syrup race in order.
items: Lift the tray onto the books and start the stopwatch
Put the same amount of each liquid on the start line
Mark a start line and a finish line
Stop the stopwatch when each liquid crosses the finish line
a: Mark a start line and a finish line
Put the same amount of each liquid on the start line
Lift the tray onto the books and start the stopwatch
Stop the stopwatch when each liquid crosses the finish line
items.why: The lines come first, then equal amounts, then the timing, then the record.

items.p: Scientists showed in 2003 that water striders move mainly by making ripples.
items.why: False. That was the old idea. In 2003, filming showed that striders push swirls of water backwards with their legs, and the water pushes them forward.

items.p: A jar of honey usually pours more slowly in a cold December than in a hot May.
items.why: True. Colder honey has a higher viscosity, so it pours more slowly.

items.p: A liquid that flows very slowly, like honey or shampoo, is called ____.
items.why: Viscous means thick and slow to flow.

items.p: Which idea explains each one: viscosity or surface tension?
items: water makes a dome on a coin
a water strider stands on a pond
an air bubble rises slowly in honey
a thread loop snaps into a circle
warm oil runs fast in a kadai
items.why: Viscosity is about how a liquid flows. Surface tension is about the skin on top of a liquid.

items.p: Plan a fair test to find out whether salty water makes a taller dome on a coin than plain water. What will you keep the same?
items.a: Use the same coin, dried each time, and the same dropper. Make drops from the same height. Count drops for plain water and salty water, three times each, and compare the middle numbers.
items.why: A strong answer changes only one thing (salt or no salt), keeps the coin, dropper and drop height the same, and repeats each try.

items.p: Give two reasons why you cannot stand on water the way a water strider can.
items.a: I am far too heavy for the water's skin to hold up. My feet are not covered in waxy hairs, so the water wets them and they break through.
items.why: A strong answer names both weight and the water-repelling legs.

items.p: Mosquitoes spread dengue. Spreading a film of special oil on stagnant water stops mosquito larvae from breathing. Three people talk about it.

views.who: Lakshmi, a health worker in Chennai
views.says: Oil on stagnant drains saves people from dengue. That matters most.

views.who: Anjali, who studies insects in ponds
views.says: Oil also harms water striders and other small animals that live on the water's skin. Use it only where there is no other way.

views.who: Meera, a parent in a flat
views.says: The best way is to stop water from standing at all. Empty pots and coolers every week, and no oil is needed.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most, and why? Then say what one of the others gets right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view with a reason, for example Meera's, because emptying standing water stops mosquitoes without harming other animals. It also says what another gets right, for example that Lakshmi is right that dengue is dangerous, and some drains cannot be emptied.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. Health workers, insect scientists and families each see a true part of it.

items.p: Draw two zoomed-in circles: one of water particles and one of honey. Show why honey flows more slowly.
items.a: Water: small particles with space to slide. Honey: big sugar particles held close to water particles, with arrows showing them clinging.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that honey's particles hold on to each other more, so they slide past each other more slowly.

items.p: Warm honey and tapped ketchup both get runnier. Are they getting runnier for the same reason? Explain.
items.a: No. Warm honey is runnier because its particles move faster. Tapped ketchup is runnier because tapping breaks a tiny net inside it. Nothing was warmed.
items.why: A strong answer gives a different reason for each: warmth speeds up particles, and shaking breaks a net.

items.p: Many people think thick liquids are heavier. Plan a test you could do at home to check this idea.
items.a: Pour some coconut oil into a glass of water. If the oil floats, it is lighter than water, even though it is thicker. Or weigh the same cup filled with each.
items.why: A strong answer tests thickness and weight separately, and uses a thick liquid that might be light, such as oil.

applications: Cooks thicken sambar, gravies and payasam to the right viscosity with dal, coconut or rice flour.
Engine oil must stay runny enough on a cold morning and thick enough when the engine is hot.
Paint and ketchup are made to flow when pushed and stay put when left alone.
Cough syrup is made thick so it coats the throat.
Soaps and detergents weaken water's skin, so water can soak into cloth and lift out dirt.
Doctors know that thicker blood flows more slowly, which matters for the heart.
Road builders heat tar until it is runny enough to spread, and it hardens as it cools.
Health workers use thin oil films on stagnant water to stop mosquito larvae breathing.
Engineers have built small robots that skate on water like water striders.
Ink pens and printers depend on ink with just the right viscosity and surface tension.

open_questions.q: What exactly happens to the particles when a hot liquid slows down and becomes glass?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can measure it very carefully, but there is still no agreed theory that explains it fully. It is often called one of the big unsolved problems of physics.

open_questions.q: Why do some liquids, like ketchup, get runnier when shaken, while a cornflour paste gets thicker?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists understand the main idea, but working out exactly how the tiny bits arrange themselves in each mixture is still being studied.

open_questions.q: How do water striders tell apart the ripples from food, from a mate and from danger?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know they use ripple signals, and have recorded some of them. How their legs and nerves sort one ripple pattern from another is not fully known.

open_questions.q: When will the next drop fall in the pitch drop experiment?
open_questions.why_open: The flow speed changes with the weather, so nobody can say exactly. The university expected the tenth drop sometime in the 2020s.

open_questions.q: Can we predict the viscosity of a new liquid from its particles alone?
open_questions.why_open: For simple liquids, yes, roughly. For mixtures like honey or blood, scientists still have to measure it.

maths.context: This is about the syrup race. You timed honey at room warmth and warmed honey down the same tray.
maths.problem: Honey at room warmth took 150 seconds to reach the finish line. Warmed honey took 30 seconds. How many seconds faster was the warm honey?
maths.explain: 150 minus 30 is 120. So the warm honey arrived 120 seconds sooner. That is 2 whole minutes, because 60 + 60 = 120.
maths.why_maths: Taking one time away from the other tells you exactly how big the difference is.

maths.context: This is about the syrup race again, with the same two honey times.
maths.problem: Honey at room warmth took 150 seconds. Warmed honey took 30 seconds. How many times as fast was the warm honey?
maths.explain: 150 divided by 30 is 5. Check: 30 + 30 + 30 + 30 + 30 = 150. So the warm honey covered the track 5 times in the time the room-warm honey covered it once.

chart.title: Time to the finish line (made-up results)

maths.why_maths: Saying 'five times as fast' tells you how much warmth changed the honey, in a way that works for any track length.

maths.context: This is about the coin drop experiment. You counted how many drops of water fit on a coin, three times.
maths.problem: Nila counted 26, 31 and 28 drops of plain water on her coin. Which is the middle number? Why is it a good number to use?
maths.explain: In order, the numbers are 26, 28, 31. The middle one is 28. One try can be a fluke, for example a drop that splashed. The middle number is not pulled up or down by one odd try.
maths.why_maths: Putting the numbers in order and picking the middle one gives a fair number when your tries are a little different.

maths.context: This is about the syrup race. Honey crawled at a steady speed down the tray.
maths.problem: Honey took 150 seconds to flow 15 centimetres. If it keeps the same speed, how long would it take to flow down a tray 30 centimetres long?
maths.explain: 30 centimetres is 2 lots of 15 centimetres. So it takes 2 lots of 150 seconds: 150 + 150 = 300 seconds. 300 seconds is 5 minutes, because 5 × 60 = 300. A real honey blob may slow down as it spreads thinner, so test it.
maths.why_maths: Using equal groups lets you predict a result before you test it, and then check if your prediction was right.

maths.context: This is about the pitch drop experiment from the How we found out card. Thomas Parnell poured hot pitch into a funnel and waited.
maths.problem: Thomas Parnell poured the pitch in 1927. He opened the funnel in 1930. The first drop fell in 1938. How many years after the pitch was poured did the first drop fall?
maths.explain: From 1927 to 1930 is 3 years. From 1930 to 1938 is 8 years. 3 + 8 = 11 years. You can also do 1938 − 1927 = 11.
maths.why_maths: Working out how long something took, from its start and end dates, shows just how slowly the pitch flows.

roots.context: We have raced liquids and watched the water's skin hold up a dome of drops. Now we ask what thick and runny liquids tell us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: The same honey crawled down your plate at room warmth and ran fast once warmed. Warmth makes a liquid's particles jiggle harder, so they slip past each other more easily. So a liquid's thickness depends on how warm it is, as well as on what it is made of.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'honey is thick' and 'water is runny' as if thickness were a fixed part of each, like a name. But thickness is how easily particles slide past each other, and that changes with warmth. The same honey can crawl or run.
deep_truth.evidence: In the syrup race, two spoons from the same honey jar raced side by side. The only difference was five minutes in warm water. The warmed honey reached the finish line several times faster.

three.who_am_i: Your blood is a liquid too. Its viscosity matters: your heart pumps it through tubes thinner than a hair.
three.what_is_life: A water strider lives their whole life on the water's skin. They find food and send signals through ripples on it.
three.what_is_this_world: Even things that look solid flow, given time: pitch in a funnel, the ice of a glacier, the hot rock deep under the ground.

roots.thread: Thick and runny, skin and no skin, all come from one thing: particles that attract each other and keep moving. In honey, they cling and slide slowly. At the top of water, the same kind of pull makes a skin a strider can stand on. Warmth shakes the particles harder and loosens their hold. So the flowing honey, the dome on the coin and the skating strider are one set of particles, holding on and letting go.

science.text: Warming lowers the viscosity of almost every liquid, because faster-moving particles slide past each other more easily.
Surface tension comes from the attraction between particles of a liquid. Soap weakens it.
Pitch flows, about 100 billion times more slowly than water.
What exactly happens to particles when a liquid slows into a glass has no agreed explanation yet.

other_view.view: Viscosity is a number we measure, and the particle picture is a useful model of it. Honey flowing faster when warm is a fact about honey. It carries no lesson about stillness or change, and reading one into it says more about us than about honey.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home today, with the materials listed. The syrup race uses half a teaspoon per lane on a tray about 30 centimetres long, raised about 8 centimetres. On that slope water finishes in a second or two, oil in a few seconds, shampoo in under a minute, and honey at room warmth in one to four minutes, depending on the honey and the room. Warmed honey is clearly faster. The warm water is bath-warm, made by a grown-up. Coconut oil that has gone hard in a cold room is warmed first. The coin test works with a straw dropper. A one-rupee coin holds roughly 15 to 40 drops of plain water, and soapy water clearly fewer. The coin must be dried well after soap. The thread loop and soap boat need fresh water for every try, because soap spreads over the whole surface. The ripple activity may be hard to feel, so watching paper squares is the fallback. The bubble race needs clear bottles, and is only a rough comparison because bottle sizes differ. No step needs a garden, a pond or a living insect, so the spine works in a city flat. Timings were checked step by step, and the spine fits about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: How did anyone find out that something hard enough to shatter can still flow? This card tells the story.
how_we_found_out.who: Thomas Parnell, the first physics professor at the University of Queensland, and John Mainstone, who looked after the experiment after him
how_we_found_out.when: 1927 (the pitch was poured), 1930 (the funnel was opened) and 1938 (the first drop fell)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People thought pitch was a solid, because it feels hard and shatters into sharp pieces when hit with a hammer. The dripping funnel showed that it flows, only extremely slowly.
how_we_found_out.story: Pitch is a black material made from tar, once used to keep boats from leaking. At room temperature it feels hard. Hit it with a hammer, and it shatters into sharp pieces, like glass. So most people thought pitch was a solid. In 1927, Thomas Parnell, a physics professor in Brisbane, Australia, wanted to show his students that it was not so simple. He heated some pitch until it was soft and poured it into a glass funnel with its stem sealed. He let it settle for three years. In 1930 he cut off the end of the stem, and waited. Nothing seemed to happen. Slowly, a drop began to grow under the funnel. The first drop fell in 1938, eight years later. Parnell died before he saw one fall. John Mainstone looked after the funnel for 52 years and also never saw a drop fall, though he came close. By 2014, nine drops had fallen. The pitch has been flowing all along, about 100 billion times more slowly than water.
